ai-agent: A single wide scene set inside a circular fence of dashed lines — the limits set by its designers. At the center, a human hand passes down a small glowing flag bearing a bullseye: a goal and nothing more, while a rolled scroll of step-by-step instructions lies discarded and unopened beside it, and at the far left, for contrast, a crumpled chat bubble has traded one question for one answer and gone dark. In the foreground a lone robot-like agent stands at a chalkboard drawing its own numbered plan beneath a clock whose hands have swept round many times, ringed by floating tool icons — a code editor, a search magnifier — while a curved arrow carries each finished attempt back through its own lens-shaped eye for a self-check and out again for another try; nearby, a dotted detour shows it chasing a mirage of a tempting wrong answer, and a tight loop of footprints shows it repeating itself, before both trails rejoin the board. A human overseer on a low platform gently nudges it back inside the fence, and a second agent with a red reviewer's pen inspects the same work. Behind them, thousands of tiny identical agents swarm over one vast, fast-rising structure, passing folded notes along dotted lines that split the labor like a team's, their speed rendered as motion streaks; at the back, a small control-room window holds a few wide-eyed humans whose slow, narrow beam of light is visibly being outpaced by the streaking swarm — and in one far corner the dashed fence bows under the crowd pressing against it.
millennium-prize-problems: A single panoramic illustration of a vast, dim hall whose rear wall holds seven colossal sealed doors, each carved with the emblem of its own problem — a turbulent, rippling wave for the question of how fluids behave, a shimmering line of glowing primes for the Riemann hypothesis, and other symbols showing that the list mixes famous old puzzles with questions at the foundations of physics — and each hung with a brass tag stamped $1,000,000, beneath a carved dedication naming the Clay Mathematics Institute and the year 2000. The only route to any door is one long, narrow bridge labeled verification: proposed proofs cross it as manuscripts riding a slow conveyor beneath a huge hourglass marked two years, while mathematicians crowd both rails with red pens, visibly tearing at and probing every page, and a carved motto above the doors declares that a proof is not a result until the community has failed to break it. One door, the Poincaré, stands open in warm light, yet at its threshold an untouched stack of banded cash and a Fields Medal sit on the floor while a lone, casually dressed figure — Perelman — walks away down the hall, empty-handed. Before the six still-sealed doors, two kinds of arrivals queue to enter that same slow bridge: human researchers clutching hand-lettered manuscripts, and, newer and glossier, corporate machines stamped with AI logos waving banners that blare the word solved, each stamped over in red with the word claim — their papers shunted onto the identical conveyor, the scene making plain that an announcement is only a claim until the slow crossing runs its course.
navier-stokes-equations: The illustration is a single wide panel that reads left to right like one continuous sentence. Across the top, the Navier–Stokes equations are written in flowing chalk-white notation that seems to pour downward into the scene and become the fluid it describes. On the left, that fluid moves in clean, parallel streamlines through three stacked everyday settings — water gliding through a pipe, air curving over an airplane wing, blood pulsing through a branching vessel — while beneath them a contented engineer with a slide rule reads numbers off the orderly flow, representing the approximate solutions used every day. Moving right, the streamlines begin to wobble, then coil into dense, chaotic eddies of turbulence, drawn ever tighter until they become a tangled scribble that the falling equation-symbols reach toward but cannot grasp, embodying the turbulence the equations seem to contain but not explain. At the far right edge, the scribble tightens to a single brilliant point where the streamlines converge and shatter, the infinity symbol ∞ bursting from it in jagged fragments beneath a large hovering question mark — the possible blow-up, where predicted speeds run to infinity and the description would break down. A gold medallion on a ribbon, stamped "Millennium Prize Problem," hangs beside that question mark, and a chalk-dusted mathematician stands at the boundary between the smooth left side and the chaotic right, hand raised as if to answer, but unable to decide.
tokens-and-pricing: A wide horizontal illustration that reads left to right like an assembly line: at the far left, a sheet of mixed writing—an ordinary sentence, a snippet of programming code, one long unfamiliar word—is fed into a slicing machine shaped like a paper cutter, which chops it into small tile-like pieces, each printed with a single token ("the", "cat", "believ", "able", "x =", "2"), every incoming tile stamped on its corner with a small coin; the tiles vanish into the machine's dark interior, and from a slot on its right side new tiles emerge one at a time, each stamped with a noticeably larger coin, sliding together to assemble a finished line of reply text, making visible that everything the model says comes out token by token, priced as it goes. Above the machine hangs a gauge that is half odometer and half cash register, its twin counters clicking upward in lockstep—one line tallying tokens, the line beneath it tallying dollars—with a small placard reading "work done / bill to pay," capturing the double meaning of a token count. A thick cable runs from the machine through a window at the upper right, opening onto a vast warehouse of humming server racks stretching to the horizon, its wall meters reading "billions of tokens" above a running total of millions of dollars, with power lines overhead and a calendar page whose days flip past to show the continuous days-long scale of a large effort. In the lower foreground, a small balance scale weighs two towers of token tiles of visibly different shapes and densities against each other, captioned "an imperfect comparison—models differ in efficiency—yet still the most concrete public yardstick of an AI project's size and cost."
